statement: In one laboratory study of a three-reagent colour kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents; a DanceSafe kit bought online, without lot numbers), compared with GC-MS or the known identity of the drugs, readings by experienced analysts matched whether MDMA was present, readings by two testers new to the kit did not, and a positive reading never showed a second drug. Three experienced analysts using the kit's instructions and colour charts read all 35 seized samples that contained MDMA as positive and the four without MDMA as negative, except that one analyst read one of the four, which held no identifiable drug, as weakly positive (editors' Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35 of 35, 51.0–100% for 4 of 4); the seven MDMA samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA read like the rest. Two testers trained in pharmacology but new to the kit, given eight samples of known drugs and only the kit's leaflet, diverged: one read both MDMA samples as negative, the other read codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan and morphine as MDMA or MDMA-like; together 2 of 4 MDMA readings were positive and 7 of 12 non-MDMA readings negative, and with the Marquis reagent alone 10 of the 12 non-MDMA readings were positive (Murray et al., 2003). A laboratory comparison from an unpublished thesis, known only from a narrative review (156 amnesty-bin samples, Marquis read by laboratory staff before GC-MS), found the MDMA colour (purple, blue or black) in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others, while the amphetamine colour appeared in 21 samples without amphetamine; its table holds 187 entries for 156 samples (Winstock et al., 2001). Two narrative reviews add, second-hand, that colour tests are presumptive: MDMA, MDEA and MDA give similar colours, other substances react too (the Marquis reagent also with aspirin and sugar), more than one drug or tablet dyes can change the result, and the tests show no amount (Winstock et al., 2001; Philp & Fu, 2018). No sample contained PMA, MDA or methamphetamine on its own, and the kit and drug market were those of the early 2000s. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one laboratory study from 2003, experts reading a three-reagent colour kit got MDMA right in all 35 samples that had it, and nearly always right in the 4 without it. But the colour looked the same when another drug was mixed in, and two people new to the kit made many mistakes, calling several other drugs MDMA. Colour tests cannot show how much MDMA is in a pill.
population: 39 police and laboratory evidence samples sold as MDMA and eight samples of known drugs (one US laboratory, early 2000s); 156 amnesty-bin samples from a London dance venue (second-hand)
exposure: A three-reagent colour test kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke, Simon's), read by experienced analysts or by two testers new to the kit; the Marquis reagent in the second-hand comparison
comparator: GC-MS of the same samples, or the known identity of the drugs supplied
outcome: Agreement of colour readings with laboratory results on whether MDMA or an MDMA-like substance was present, and what the readings did not show
magnitude: Murray et al. Part I (experienced analysts, three reagents): 35/35 MDMA samples positive (Wilson 90.1–100%, editors' calculation); 4/4 non-MDMA negative for two analysts (51.0–100%), 3/4 for the third (one weak positive); 7 samples with a second drug read like MDMA alone. Part II (two novices, 8 known drugs, three reagents): sensitivity 2/4 (50%), specificity 7/12 (58%), positive and negative predictive values 2/7 and 7/9 (printed 28% and 77%); Novice A 0/2 MDMA detected and 5/6 others negative, Novice B 2/2 and 2/6; Marquis alone 10 false positives in 12 non-MDMA readings and 2 false negatives. Winstock et al. (second-hand, Murphy 1999): purple/blue/black 53/53 MDMA-like and 0 others; orange/brown 47 amphetamine samples and 21 without; 187 cell entries for n = 156.

evidence.locator: Table 2 and footnote (p. 1240); Results › Part I, 1st paragraph (p. 1241)
evidence.extracted: Three analysts, experienced chemists familiar with reagent use, tested with Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents: each recorded 35 positives; GC-MS found MDMA in all 35, seven of them also with caffeine, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA. Of the four samples without MDMA (alprazolam; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with guaifenesin; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with caffeine; no identifiable drug), Analysts 2 and 3 recorded four negatives and Analyst 1 three negatives and one weak positive (the sample with no identifiable drug). The analysts disagreed on exact colours but generally agreed on whether MDMA was present; Marquis alone gave similar results, not shown. Editors' calculation: Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35/35 and 51.0–100% for 4/4.

evidence.locator: Results › Part II, 1st paragraph; Table 3 and footnotes
evidence.extracted: Two testers, professionals in pharmacology and toxicology inexperienced with the kits, given the kit, its labelling and eight blinded samples (codeine, dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine, ketamine, MDMA twice, morphine, d-norpropoxyphene): sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values 50%, 58%, 28% and 77% for both testers together with all three reagents. Novice A called only morphine positive (for an MDMA-like substance) and both MDMA samples negative; Novice B called all but ketamine and d-norpropoxyphene positive for MDMA or an MDMA-like substance. With Marquis alone each tester had five false positives, and Novice A two false negatives. One tester was slightly injured by a drop of reagent.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Part I Testing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 1239–1240); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 1243)
evidence.extracted: Two identical kits were bought from an Internet source, without lot numbers to check; Part I used samples sold as MDMA and held as evidence, chosen from two sources for variety, read in timed batches with the kit's instructions and colour charts by one analyst while a second observed; the authors acknowledge possible selection and analyst bias and call the 39 samples relatively small.

evidence.locator: Table 3; Comparison of the Marquis test with GC-MS analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand, from an MSc thesis (Murphy, 1999): 156 samples left anonymously in an amnesty bin at a London dance venue, Marquis tested by laboratory staff blind to the initial results before GC-MS. Purple/blue/black readings occurred in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in none of the others; orange/brown in all 47 amphetamine samples and in 21 others; yellow/green (the 2C-B colour) in 8 and purple/violet (the opiate colour) in 14 with no matching GC-MS class; 44 gave no colour and held none of the listed classes; the 2C-B readings were explained by diphenhydramine. Editors' sum: the table's cells add to 187, not 156.

evidence.locator: The process of pill testing, 3rd to 5th paragraphs (p. 1143); Table 2 (p. 1144); The usefulness of pill testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 1145)
evidence.extracted: Narrative critique: Marquis colours are read subjectively and change over time; when more than one drug is present the colours mix; many substances react with sulphuric acid alone; diphenhydramine gives the same colour as 2C-B; Table 2, from a forensic reference, lists violet-purple to blue-black for MDMA and MDEA and blue-black for MDA; colour tests give no information on the strength of a pill and cannot tell optical isomers apart.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (AM p. 2); Chemistry of common color tests › General screening reagents, 1st paragraph (AM p. 4); Limitations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (AM p. 10)
evidence.extracted: Narrative review: colour tests are presumptive and sit in SWGDRUG's lowest discriminating-power category (C); the Marquis reagent also reacts with aspirin and sugar; results may be affected by more than one drug in a sample or by colouring agents in tablets such as ecstasy; tablets seized in Italy and presumptively identified as amphetamines with Marquis contained two anabolic steroids and no amphetamine-type substance.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Philp_2018_SpotTestsReview.pdf (accepted manuscript; AM p. = PDF page)

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for Murray et al. (study card): evidence samples chosen for variety, readers who knew the samples were sold as MDMA, no stated reading rule, and a rule for 'MDMA-like' readings fixed at analysis; the second-hand table's methods cannot be checked.

inconsistency.note: Experienced laboratory readings agree in both datasets; the novice results differ by condition, not by conflict.

indirectness.note: A 2003 kit read in a laboratory, seized samples of the early 2000s with no PMA, MDA or methamphetamine on its own, and newer substances untested; the novice part used legitimate medicines rather than street drugs.

imprecision.note: Four samples without MDMA in the experienced part (interval 51 to 100 in 100); two novice testers and eight samples.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high and is rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, so very low. Rated as worded: agreement of colour readings with laboratory analysis in these conditions; whether colour testing changes what people do is a separate question. Status single study: Murray et al. is the only primary study read; the amnesty-bin comparison is known only second-hand, from an unpublished thesis tabulated in a narrative review, and points the same way for laboratory readers. The narrative reviews (Winstock et al.; Philp & Fu) qualify the claim and are labelled second-hand.
